title: Dominic and the Letters Again
premise: Marguerite Oyelaran, a wedding planner who swore off love after his mother's death and a betrayal he never named aloud, is hired to plan the Harvest Festival wedding at Bellamy Orchard—only to discover the deed lists him as co-inheritor alongside Dominic Ashford, the man who broke his heart ten years ago and vanished. The orchard belonged to Marguerite's late mother, who secretly kept in touch with Dominic through letters Marguerite never knew existed. As the festival deadline forces the two men to restore the orchard together, Marguerite reads the letters one by one, learning that his mother orchestrated their reunion and that Dominic left to protect him from a scandal that ruined both families. At the festival's final night, Marguerite must choose between selling the orchard and erasing the past, or forgiving himself and Dominic—choosing, at last, to stay.
about_author: Sable Sterling is the pen name of a former estate lawyer who left practice after handling one too many inheritance disputes that were really love stories in disguise. They write romance from a converted apple barn in the Hudson Valley, where they keep a drawer of other people's unsent letters.

chapters.title: The Deed That Wouldn't Die
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A meticulous wedding planner takes what should be an easy festival contract at Bellamy Orchard, then discovers his own name on the deed beside a name he swore he'd buried: Dominic Ashford. The beat is cold shock masked as professional calm.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Good Posture
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Flashback-tinged chapter establishing the heart-as-muscle philosophy: his mother's death, the betrayal he refuses to name, and the wedding he walked out of—his own. Ends with him deciding to take the job anyway, 'purely professionally.' Emotional beat: denial.

chapters.title: The Man in the Row of Apples
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic returns to the orchard expecting paperwork and a quick signature, instead finding Marguerite directing vendors like a general. Their first collision is all clipped civility and old electricity. Beat: the past arriving in work boots.

chapters.title: Terms of Surrender
chapters.summary: Both POVs alternate. The lawyer reveals neither man can sell without the other's signature, and the festival contract binds them to cooperate for six weeks. They negotiate a truce: no personal history, only logistics. Beat: a treaty both sides plan to violate.

chapters.title: Letter One: The Beekeeping Year
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. While clearing his mother's writing desk, he finds the first of dozens of letters—his mother writing to Dominic, warm and familiar, dated after the breakup. Marguerite reads it standing in a cold pantry. Beat: the floor tilting under a settled life.

chapters.title: Pruning Season
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Working the orchard together, Dominic teaches Marguerite to prune; Marguerite pretends not to notice how well they still fit as a team. A near-touch over the same branch. Beat: muscle memory of tenderness.

chapters.title: Letter Two: What You Did for Him
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The second letter hints that Dominic's disappearance was a sacrifice, not abandonment—'what you did for him, he must never learn from me.' Marguerite burns with questions he won't ask. Beat: suspicion turning inward.

chapters.title: The Rehearsal Dinner Nobody Rehearsed
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The festival couple's disastrous tasting forces Marguerite and Dominic to co-host; a drunk grandmother toasts 'to second chances' and the room looks at them. Beat: public embarrassment, private ache.

chapters.title: Letter Three: The Scandal
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic rereads his own unsent reply, and we learn the truth: his father embezzled from Marguerite's mother's business, and Dominic left to testify against his own family quietly, sparing Marguerite the trial. Beat: guilt kept like a stone in the shoe.

chapters.title: Storm Damage
chapters.summary: Both POVs. A storm wrecks the festival tent and half the orchard; the two men work through the night sandbagging and salvaging, and Marguerite laughs for the first time in years. Beat: intimacy through shared labor.

chapters.title: Letter Four: The Matchmaker's Confession
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A letter reveals his mother knew Dominic's secret all along and forgave it—and asks Dominic to look after Marguerite 'when he finally stops being furious.' Marguerite realizes he's been grieving the wrong betrayal. Beat: grief rearranging itself.

chapters.title: The Almost
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. After the storm cleanup, wine, and a power outage, they nearly kiss—until Marguerite pulls back, saying 'I don't forgive you,' though the letter has already told him there's nothing to forgive. Beat: fear wearing anger's clothing.

chapters.title: Letter Five: The One I Never Sent You
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. He finds a letter his mother wrote to him, never sent, asking him to stop punishing himself for his father's debts and his own cold feet. He reads it aloud to the empty kitchen. Beat: the mirror begins to crack.

chapters.title: Rival Bids
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A developer's aggressive offer tempts Marguerite—sell, walk away, stay invisible. Dominic, hurt, signs nothing and withdraws. Beat: the old reflex to flee, offered a legal exit.

chapters.title: The Wedding That Isn't Theirs
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic attends the festival couple's ceremony rehearsal alone and watches Marguerite make two strangers' love look inevitable, understanding that Marguerite has been planning funerals for his own heart for a decade. Beat: tenderness as evidence.

chapters.title: Letter Six: The Last Instruction
chapters.summary: Both POVs converge. The final letter, addressed to both men, names her wish: the orchard to both of them, together or not at all, 'because you were never finished.' Marguerite confronts Dominic with everything. Beat: the truth, finally spoken aloud.

chapters.title: What You Did for Me
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic tells the whole story of the testimony, the ruin, the silence. Marguerite's fury collapses into something worse and better: understanding. Beat: anger running out of places to hide.

chapters.title: The Festival Eve
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Everything goes wrong before the festival—vendors lost, the couple fighting, the tent leaking—and Marguerite, for once, asks for help instead of performing competence. Dominic stays. Beat: vulnerability as strength.

chapters.title: Climax: The Question in the Orchard
chapters.summary: Both POVs. At the festival's peak, before the whole town, Marguerite stops the music—not for the couple, but to publicly sign the co-inheritance, keep the orchard, and ask Dominic, badly and trembling, to stay and try again. Beat: choosing to be visible.

chapters.title: Letter Seven: Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. He reads his mother's final letter at the orchard gate at dawn, then writes one of his own—unsent, but no longer ashamed. He forgives the man in the mirror. Beat: inheritance claimed, not of land but of love.

chapters.title: The Signature
chapters.summary: Both POVs. The deed is signed, the developer refused, the festival couple married under repaired string lights. Dominic and Marguerite plant a new apple tree over the old letters, buried like seeds. Beat: quiet, earned joy.

chapters.title: Epilogue: The Next Harvest
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, one year later. The orchard hosts its first festival under their names; Marguerite plans weddings again, but this time he believes in at least one of them—his own, next spring, under the young tree. Beat: the heart, retrained, at rest.
